This BMW M5 Competition Just Sold for $16,000 – No Catch Here
15 photos
Photo: Cars&Bids
And we really mean it, there is no catch here, because as you can clearly see from the images shared below, it is the F10-generation of the BMW M5 , and some say it is the last true M5, because it was the final one to be offered strictly with rear-wheel drive.
As you likely recall, the F90 was all-wheel drive, and so is the modern-day G9X (G90 Sedan / G99 Touring). The F10 was made between 2011 and 2016, featuring a seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission mated to the familiar 4.4-liter twin-turbocharged V8 engine. The US and Canada also got a six-speed manual transmission option, but the car shown above does not have it.
The vehicle in question is a 2014 model year BMW M5 equipped with the Competition Package. Therefore, it has more oomph, enjoying 575 horsepower (583 ps/423 kW) and 502 pound-feet (680 Nm) of torque. As you already know, everything is channeled to the rear wheels, because the rear-biased xDrive all-wheel drive system was not available for this generation of the premium mid-size sedan.
The Competition Package boosted the output by 15 hp (15 ps/11 kW ), shaving one-tenth of a second from the 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 kph) sprint compared to the standard M5 of that era, and 0.2 seconds when it came to the 0 to 124 mph (0-200 kph) acceleration. From 0-62 mph, the model needed a hair over the 4-second mark, though independent testing showed that it was some half a second faster than advertised.
Flat-out, it could do 155 mph (250 kph), though if you ticked the M Driver’s Package box on the options list, then the top speed would have increased to 190 mph (305 kph).
Photo: Cars&Bids This BMW M5 boasts the Competition Package, as we already told you, and also features the Executive Package and the Driver Assistance Package. It rides on the 343M wheels, which measure 20 inches in diameter, benefits from adaptive LED headlights, has Merino leather upholstery, a power sunroof, and a premium sound system from Bang & Olufsen.
Unfortunately, it also has some modifications, though it’s nothing that cannot be easily reverted back to the OEM configuration if the new owner does not fancy them, because these included the painted front reflectors, and the black kidney grilles.
But what about the known flaws, you ask? Well, this BMW M5 has some wear on the seats and interior surfaces, as you can see in the images shared in the gallery, as well as curb rash on the wheels. There are also some chips and scratches on the outside, and paint damage on the front bumper.
According to the seller, who reportedly bought this machine in July 2026, adding some 5,000 miles (~8,000 km), the car “ drives very good, ” and the “ last owner took good care of it. ” At the time of cataloging, this ride had 118,500 miles (190,700 km) on the clock, so it is a high-mileage example.
The current market value of a high-mileage BMW M5 from the 2014 model year is between $20,000 and $25,000, though vehicles with over 90,000 miles (145,000 km) in rough usually change hands for roughly $20,000. Vehicles in good condition with some 50,000 to 80,000 miles (80,000-129,000 km) usually go from $26,000 to $35,000, and low-mileage machines with less than 40,000 miles (~65,000 km) can cost close to $50,000.
Photo: Cars&Bids It is worth noting that the Competition Package models usually fetch a $3,000 to $5,000 premium in today’s used car market in the United States of America. Therefore, in theory, this particular 2014 BMW M5 Competition should have gone for around $25,000. However, it fetched a lot less, because as we already told you in the title, it went for $16,000.
The business super sedan , which has a Singapore Gray Metallic paint finish on the outside and a black interior, was advertised on Cars&Bids as part of an online auction that ended on November 3, 2026. The car failed to sell when the gavel hit the table, but it changed hands shortly after for the aforementioned sum.
It has a clean Arizona title, a clean Carfax history report showing that it has no mileage discrepancies and has never been involved in an accident, and has been registered mostly in California since it left the dealership back in the day. Besides the car, the next owner will get a spare set of floor mats, and one key, the listing reveals.
Now, paying $16K for a great business super sedan is definitely a win, in my book anyway, because this is a lot of car for the money, so congrats to the new owner. But if you came across this F10 BMW M5 Competition listed for $16K, would you have bought it?
